statement: Find a triangle whose three side lengths and an altitude are four consecutive integers, where the altitude splits it into two integer-sided right triangles. Prove uniqueness.
solution: Write the altitude as $h$. The two incident sides exceed $h$, so they lie among $h+1,h+2,h+3$, and the base is at least $h-1$. Each horizontal leg of the two right triangles is at most $\sqrt{(h+3)^2-h^2}=\sqrt{6h+9}$. Hence $h-1\le2\sqrt{6h+9}$, giving $h^2-26h-35\le0$ and therefore $h\le27$. Checking $h=1,\ldots,27$ and side $s=h+1,h+2,h+3$ for square $s^2-h^2$ gives exactly $(h,s,\text{other leg})=(3,5,4),(4,5,3),(8,10,6),(12,13,5),(12,15,9),(15,17,8),(24,25,7),(24,26,10)$. Two distinct incident sides at one height are possible only for $h=12$ or 24. At 12, the legs 5 and 9 sum to 14, giving sides 13,14,15. At 24, the legs 7 and 10 sum to 17, inconsistent with four consecutive lengths. Thus the unique triangle has sides 13,14,15 and altitude 12.
ratingReason: A geometric size bound makes the integer search finite and small; checking integer right-triangle legs leaves two heights, and the base condition singles out one.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: Prove that a real number $x$ is rational exactly when three distinct terms of $x,x+1,x+2,\ldots$ form a geometric progression.
solution: If $x+i,x+j,x+k$ form a geometric progression, then $(x+j)^2=(x+i)(x+k)$, so $(2j-i-k)x=ik-j^2$. The coefficient cannot vanish: if it did, $i+k=2j$ and $ik=j^2$ would force $i=j=k$. Thus $x$ is rational. Conversely write $x=a/b$ with integers $a$ and $b>0$. Choose $N\ge0$ so $r=x+N=c/b>0$. The three numbers $r,r(b+1),r(b+1)^2$ have successive offsets from $r$ equal to $0,c,c(b+2)$, all nonnegative integers. They are distinct terms of the original sequence and form a geometric progression.
ratingReason: The forward implication needs to rule out a vanishing coefficient; the converse constructs terms even when the original rational number is negative.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: In triangle $ABC$, the medians to $AB$ and $AC$ are perpendicular. Prove $\cot B+\cot C\ge2/3$.
solution: Put the centroid at the origin and the two perpendicular median lines on the coordinate axes. Then $B=(p,0)$, $C=(0,q)$, and $A=(-p,-q)$, with $pq\ne0$. Thus $BC^2=p^2+q^2$ and twice the area is $3|pq|$. In any triangle, $\cot B+\cot C=BC^2/(2[ABC])$, by projecting the altitude onto $BC$. Therefore $\cot B+\cot C=(p^2+q^2)/(3|pq|)\ge2/3$, with equality when $|p|=|q|$.
ratingReason: The centroid makes the perpendicular-median condition into coordinate axes; the cotangent sum becomes a simple squared-length ratio.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: Players from different schools each play one tennis match; players from the same school do not meet. The total numbers of boys and girls differ by at most one, and the number of same-sex matches differs from the number of mixed matches by at most one. What is the greatest possible number of schools with an odd number of players?
solution: For school $i$, put $d_i=b_i-g_i$, and let $D=\sum_i d_i$. Then $|D|\le1$. The difference between same-sex and mixed matches is $\sum_{i<j}d_i d_j=(D^2-\sum_i d_i^2)/2$, whose absolute value is at most 1. Hence $\sum_i d_i^2\le D^2+2\le3$. Every odd-sized school has odd, nonzero $d_i$, contributing at least 1, so there are at most three. Three schools containing one boy, one boy, and one girl attain the bound: there is one same-sex match and two mixed matches.
ratingReason: Encoding each school by its gender imbalance turns both global balance conditions into a sum-of-squares bound that counts odd-sized schools.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: Define $y_1=1$. For $k\ge1$, set $(y_{2k},y_{2k+1})=(2y_k,2y_k+1)$ when $k$ is even, and $(2y_k+1,2y_k)$ when $k$ is odd. Prove that every positive integer occurs exactly once in the sequence.
solution: Induct on binary length to show $y_n=n\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, where xor adds each binary digit modulo 2 without carrying. Appending a bit $b$ to the binary representation of $k$ appends to this xor value the bit $b$ xor the last bit of $k$, exactly as in the recurrence. This map is invertible: if the output bits from most significant to least are $c_m,\ldots,c_0$, recover the input bits by $b_m=c_m$ and $b_i=c_i$ xor $b_{i+1}$. The leading bit remains 1, so the inverse gives one positive integer for every positive output.
ratingReason: The parity-dependent recursion is an adjacent-bit transform. An explicit inverse, rather than mere injectivity on initial blocks, proves every positive value occurs exactly once.
notes: Statement restated in original wording. Official CMS paper checked; original independent proof supplied because no worked solution is linked in the official archive.

statement: Nine teams play a round-robin tournament, with no drawn games. A team earns one point for each win. Every team with at most two points is eliminated. What is the largest possible number of eliminated teams?
ratingReason: Count the games played solely among eliminated teams to bound their number; a regular five-team tournament provides the matching construction.

solution: If $k$ teams are eliminated, their internal games already contribute $k(k-1)/2$ wins, whereas they have at most $2k$ wins in total. Hence $k\le5$. To attain five, arrange the five teams cyclically and let each beat the next two and lose to the other two; let all five lose to each of the remaining four teams. Thus the maximum is $5$.

statement: Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and $AB=2BC$. A point $D$ on the internal bisector of $\angle ABC$ satisfies $AD=DC$. Prove that the line through $A$ perpendicular to $BD$ bisects segment $DC$.

solution: Scale so that $B=(0,0),A=(2,0),C=(0,1)$. Write $D=(t,t)$. The equation $AD^2=DC^2$ gives $(t-2)^2+t^2=t^2+(t-1)^2$, hence $t=3/2$. The midpoint of $DC$ is $(3/4,5/4)$, lying on $x+y=2$, the perpendicular to $BD$ through $A$.

statement: Let $f(x)=1/x$ and $g(x)=1-x$. Find $(g\circ f)^{100}(2013)$, where the superscript denotes repeated composition.

solution: For $h=g\circ f$, $h(x)=(x-1)/x$, $h^2(x)=1/(1-x)$ and $h^3(x)=x$. The orbit of $2013$ avoids the undefined values. Since $100\equiv1\pmod3$, the answer is $2012/2013$.

statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer and $p$ a prime such that $p\nmid(3n)!$ but $p\mid(3n+1)!+(3n+2)!$. Prove that $3\mid p-1$.

solution: We have $p>3n$ and the sum factors as $(3n)!(3n+1)(3n+3)$. A prime divisor of $3n+3=3(n+1)$ is at most $\max(3,n+1)\le3n$. Therefore $p\mid3n+1$. Since $p>3n$, this forces $p=3n+1$.

statement: An equilateral triangle of side $7$ is divided into unit equilateral triangles. ratingReason: The local colouring rule forces a periodic triangular-lattice colouring. Counting the equal colour classes then gives the matching identity.

solution: The colour of any adjacent pair forces the colour of the third vertex, so the colouring is the standard periodic three-colouring, up to permutation. Rows of lengths $1,2,\ldots,8$ contain $12$ vertices of each colour (this follows by listing the three residues in each row). If $x,y,z$ count red–blue, red–green and blue–green edges, respectively, counting blue and green vertices gives $x+z=12=y+z$, so $x=y$.

statement: Prove that $4a^2+2b^4+c^8+d^8\ge8abcd$ for positive real numbers $a,b,c,d$.

statement: Prove that there do not exist $2015$ integers whose sum and product are both $2015$.

statement: A permutation of $1,2,\ldots,n$ is called magical if every entry $j$ has at least $\lfloor j/2\rfloor$ smaller entries to its left. Determine the number of magical permutations.
ratingReason: Insert entries in increasing order: the condition for the new largest entry gives an independent number of slots and does not affect older entries.

solution: Insert $j$ into a magical permutation of $1,\ldots,j-1$. Of the $j$ slots, precisely $j-\lfloor j/2\rfloor=\lceil j/2\rceil$ have enough smaller entries to the left. Previous conditions are unchanged. Hence the answer is $\prod_{j=1}^n\lceil j/2\rceil=\lfloor n/2\rfloor!\,\lceil n/2\rceil!$.

statement: For a positive integer $n$, let $d(n)$ be its number of positive divisors. Prove that $d(a)+d(b)\le d(\gcd(a,b))+d(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b))$ for all positive integers $a,b$, and determine all equality cases.
ratingReason: Viewing divisors as sets makes the inequality an inclusion–exclusion statement. The equality classification requires noticing when the least common multiple belongs to the union.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Let $D(m)$ be the set of positive divisors of $m$. Then $D(a)\cap D(b)=D(\gcd(a,b))$ and $D(a)\cup D(b)\subseteq D(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b))$. Inclusion–exclusion gives the inequality. Equality means the union is the latter entire set, so the least common multiple itself divides $a$ or $b$. Thus equality holds exactly when $a\mid b$ or $b\mid a$, which also plainly suffices.

statement: A sequence of real numbers $a_1,a_2,\ldots$ satisfies $a_1>0$ and $a_1a_2\cdots a_n=a_1+\cdots+a_{n-1}$ for every $n\ge2$. What is the maximum possible number of integer terms in the sequence?
ratingReason: Dividing consecutive product–sum identities gives a monotonic reciprocal recurrence. After the first few terms, a short interval contains no integers, leaving a finite endpoint analysis.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Put $t=a_1>0$ and $S_k=a_1+\cdots+a_k$. The identities give $a_2=1$, $a_3=a_4=1+1/t$, and, by dividing consecutive identities, $a_{n+1}=1+a_n/S_{n-1}$. In particular $a_5=1+1/(t+1)$ lies strictly between $1$ and $2$. Since $S_3=t+2+1/t\ge4$ and all terms are positive, the same recurrence inductively keeps every $a_n$ with $n\ge5$ strictly between $1$ and $2$. Thus only the first four terms can be integers. Setting $t=1$ makes them $1,1,2,2$, so the maximum is $4$.

statement: Initially there are ten piles of stones, of sizes $1,2,\ldots,10$. A move either merges two piles of at least two stones and adds two stones to the result, or takes two stones from a pile of at least four and splits the remainder into two nonempty piles. Play stops when no move is possible. (a) Give a sequence that stops. (b) Tabulate the number of piles and total stones initially and after your first five moves. (c) Prove that every terminal position has the same number of one-stone piles.
ratingReason: The linear invariant total stones plus twice the number of piles determines the terminal singleton count after a short classification of possible terminal positions.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Let $S$ be the number of stones and $P$ the number of piles. Both moves preserve $S+2P=75$. At termination all piles have size at most three and at most one has size greater than one. If there are $k$ singleton piles, the invariant gives either $3k=75$, $3k+4=75$, or $3k+5=75$. Only the first is possible, and $k=25$. For a terminating sequence, repeatedly split any pile of size $m\ge4$ into sizes $1,m-3$ after removing two stones. This strictly reduces $S$. When only piles of sizes 1,2,3 remain, merge two nonsingleton piles if present, then resume splitting; this reduces their number. Starting by splitting piles $10,9,8,7,6$ gives $(P,S)=(10,55),(11,53),(12,51),(13,49),(14,47),(15,45)$. Continue the described process to reach 25 singletons.

statement: A square $ABCD$ has side length $60$. Points $M\in AD$ and $N\in CD$ are chosen so that $BM$ and $BN$ divide the square into three regions of equal area. Find $DM$ and $DN$.

statement: A diamond-shaped pattern of unit squares begins at step $0$ with one square. At step $1$ its horizontal rows have lengths $1,3,1$; at step $2$ they have lengths $1,3,5,3,1$. statement: In triangle $ABC$, $BM$ is a median, $BC=\frac23MC$, and $\angle BMC=2\angle ABM$. Find $AB/AM$.

solution: Write $\theta=\angle ABM$. Since $\angle BMA=180^\circ-2\theta$, $\angle BAM=\theta$, so $AM=BM$. As $AM=MC$, the points $A,B,C$ lie on a circle with centre $M$ and diameter $AC$, giving $AB^2+BC^2=AC^2$. With $AM=MC=t$ and $BC=2t/3$, this gives $AB/AM=\sqrt{4-4/9}=4\sqrt2/3$.

statement: Squares constructed on the three sides of a triangular field have areas $505$, $233$ and $52$ hectares. Find the area of the triangular field.
ratingReason: The cosine rule determines the product of two sides times the cosine of their included angle; subtracting its square from the squared side product gives the area.

solution: Let $a^2=505,b^2=233,c^2=52$ and let $A$ be opposite $a$. Then $bc\cos A=(233+52-505)/2=-110$. Hence $(bc\sin A)^2=233\cdot52-110^2=16$. The area is $bc\sin A/2=2$ hectares.

statement: Two concentric circles have radii $R>r$. A chord of the larger circle, tangent to the smaller circle, has length $5$ cm. Find the area between the circles.
ratingReason: The radius to the point of tangency bisects the chord, giving the difference of the squared radii directly by Pythagoras.

solution: The right triangle formed by the common centre, chord midpoint and endpoint gives $R^2-r^2=(5/2)^2$. Hence the annulus has area $\pi(R^2-r^2)=25\pi/4$ square centimetres.

statement: Positive integers $a,b$ satisfy $\frac{a+1}{b}+\frac{b+1}{a}\in\mathbb Z$. Prove that $\gcd(a,b)\le\sqrt{a+b}$.
ratingReason: Multiplying out the integer condition exposes a+b as a multiple of the square of the gcd; positivity supplies the bound.

solution: Let $d=\gcd(a,b)$ and let the displayed integer be $K$. Then $a+b=Kab-a^2-b^2$, which is divisible by $d^2$. Since $a+b>0$, we have $a+b\ge d^2$.

statement: An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle. A point $M$ lies on the arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Prove that $MA=MB+MC$.
ratingReason: Recognising the cyclic quadrilateral as a Ptolemy configuration turns the relation into one line after cancelling equal sides.

solution: Ptolemy applied to the cyclic quadrilateral $ABMC$ gives $AM\cdot BC=AB\cdot MC+AC\cdot MB$. Since $AB=BC=CA$, division by this common positive length proves the claim.

statement: Does there exist a real number $x\in[-\pi,0]$ satisfying $2-\cos2x+2\sqrt2\cos(x-\pi/2)=0$?
ratingReason: Standard trigonometric identities complete a square in sin x, leaving a familiar exact-angle value.

solution: The left side is $1+2\sin^2x+2\sqrt2\sin x=(\sqrt2\sin x+1)^2$. It vanishes when $\sin x=-1/\sqrt2$. Thus such numbers exist: both $x=-\pi/4$ and $x=-3\pi/4$ work. The source solution overlooks the second value; the existence claim is unaffected.

statement: Compare each expression with $2$: (a) $\frac1{\log_2\pi}+\frac1{\log_5\pi}$; (b) $\frac1{\log_2\pi}+\frac1{\log_\pi2}$.
ratingReason: Changing logarithm bases simplifies the first comparison to pi squared versus ten, while the second is the elementary reciprocal AM–GM inequality.

solution: (a) The sum is $\log_\pi10>2$, since $\pi^2<10$ (for example $\pi<22/7$). (b) Put $t=\log_2\pi>0$. The expression is $t+1/t\ge2$, with equality only for $t=1$. Since $\pi\ne2$, it is strictly greater than $2$.

statement: Find all integer triples $(x,y,z)$ satisfying $xy+z=2023$ and $x+yz=2021$.
ratingReason: Subtracting the equations factors into a product equal to two, so only four signed factor pairs remain to check.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Subtracting gives $(y-1)(x-z)=2$. For $(y-1,x-z)=(1,2)$, the first equation gives $2(z+2)+z=2023$, hence $(x,y,z)=(675,2,673)$. For $(2,1)$, it gives $3(z+1)+z=2023$, hence $(506,3,505)$. For $(-1,-2)$, $y=0$ and the original equations give $(2021,0,2023)$. For $(-2,-1)$, $y=-1$ and the first equation becomes $1=2023$, impossible. These three triples satisfy both equations.

statement: Triangle $ABC$ has side lengths $5$, $12$ and $13$ cm. Find the radius of its incircle.
ratingReason: Recognising the Pythagorean triple gives the area immediately; dividing by the semiperimeter gives the inradius.

solution: The triangle is right-angled, so its area is $5\cdot12/2=30$. Its semiperimeter is $15$. Since area equals inradius times semiperimeter, the radius is $2$ cm.

statement: Find all real solutions of $2^x=\sqrt{9\cdot2^{x+2}-128}$.
ratingReason: The substitution u=2^x turns the equation into a quadratic, followed by a straightforward domain check.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Square and put $u=2^x>0$. Then $u^2=36u-128$, so $(u-4)(u-32)=0$. Thus $x=2$ or $5$. Both satisfy the original equation.

statement: A square $ABCD$ has side $2$ cm. Inside it lies a semicircle with diameter $AB$. A circle inside the square is externally tangent to this semicircle and tangent to sides $BC$ and $CD$. Find its radius.
ratingReason: The two tangencies to adjacent sides locate the centre in terms of the radius. One Pythagorean relation expresses the remaining circle tangency.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Use $A=(0,0),B=(2,0),C=(2,2),D=(0,2)$. The semicircle centre is $(1,0)$ and the smaller circle centre is $(2-r,2-r)$. External tangency gives $(1-r)^2+(2-r)^2=(1+r)^2$, or $r^2-8r+4=0$. Only $r=4-2\sqrt3$ fits inside the square.

statement: A regular hexagon $ABCDEF$ is inscribed in a circle. Points $N\in EC$ and $M\in AC$ satisfy $AM/AC=CN/CE$. A point $R$ on the circle lies on the ray $DN$ beyond $N$. The arc $EFR$ has measure $90^\circ$, and $AC=\sqrt3$. Determine $AM$.
ratingReason: The regular hexagon supplies equal chords and fixed angles. Matching the two side ratios creates congruent triangles, reducing the length to a standard right-triangle ratio.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Since $AC=CE$, we have $AM=CN$ and $CM=EN$. Also $BC=DE$ and $\angle BCM=\angle DEN=30^\circ$, so triangles $BCM$ and $DEN$ are congruent. The inscribed angle $\angle EDR$ subtends arc $EFR$, hence is $45^\circ$. Thus $\angle CBM=45^\circ$. In triangle $BCM$, the sine rule gives $CM/BC=\sin45^\circ/\sin105^\circ=\sqrt3-1$. Therefore $AM=AC-CM=\sqrt3BC-(\sqrt3-1)BC=BC=1$.

statement: Find all real $k$ for which $kx^2+k=3x^2+2-2kx$ has two distinct real roots and the sum of its roots equals their product plus $k$.
ratingReason: Vieta converts the root condition into k squared equals two; the discriminant removes the negative choice.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: The quadratic is $(k-3)x^2+2kx+k-2=0$. With $k\ne3$, Vieta gives $-2k/(k-3)=(k-2)/(k-3)+k$, hence $k^2=2$. Its discriminant is $20k-24$, which must be positive. Thus only $k=\sqrt2$ works.

statement: Find all real numbers $a$ for which the polynomial $x^3+ax-2(a+4)$ has exactly two distinct real roots.
ratingReason: A fixed root factors out at once. Exactly two real roots then requires either a repeated quadratic root or a quadratic root shared with the fixed linear factor.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Factor as $(x-2)(x^2+2x+a+4)$. If the quadratic has a repeated root, its discriminant $-4(a+3)$ vanishes, so $a=-3$; its root $-1$ differs from $2$. Otherwise it must have two distinct real roots, one of which is $2$. Substitution gives $a=-12$, with quadratic roots $2,-4$. Thus $a\in\{-3,-12\}$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: A circle with centre $O$ has diameters $AB$ and $CX$, with $OB=BC$. Its area is $315\text{ cm}^2$. Find the combined area of the two opposite minor sectors $BOC$ and $AOX$.
ratingReason: The equal chord and radius form an equilateral triangle, fixing each central angle and hence the fraction of the circle shaded.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Since $OB=OC=BC$, triangle $OBC$ is equilateral and $\angle BOC=60^\circ$. The opposite angle $AOX$ is also $60^\circ$. The two sectors therefore occupy $120/360=1/3$ of the circle, giving $105\text{ cm}^2$.

solution: For $f(x)=(x-1)/x$, $f^2(x)=1/(1-x)$ and $f^3(x)=x$. The orbit of $217$ is well-defined and repeats every three terms. Since $2017\equiv1\pmod3$, $a_{2017}=217$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: How many three-digit positive integers $\overline{ABC}$ have the property that $(A+B)^C$ is a three-digit integral power of $2$?
ratingReason: The base must be a power of two, and the exponent must yield 128,256 or512. Counting digit pairs for the resulting few bases completes the problem.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: The three-digit powers of two are $128,256,512$. Therefore $A+B$ must be one of $2,4,8,16$. For $A+B=2$, the exponents $C=7,8,9$ each allow two digit pairs, giving $6$ numbers. For $A+B=4$, only $C=4$ works, with four pairs. For $A+B=8$, only $C=3$ works, with eight pairs. For $A+B=16$, only $C=2$ works, with three pairs. Thus the total is $6+4+8+3=21$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: A regular tetrahedron has volume $724\text{ cm}^3$. At each vertex, cut it by the plane through the midpoints of the three edges from that vertex, and remove the corner tetrahedron. What volume remains?
ratingReason: Each removed corner is a half-scale copy, so its volume is one eighth of the original.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Four corners are removed, each with volume $724/8$. Thus the remaining volume is $724(1-4/8)=362\text{ cm}^3$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: A right triangle has perimeter $180$, and the sum of the squares of its three side lengths is $12800$. Find its area.
ratingReason: Pythagoras determines the hypotenuse from the sum of squares, after which the leg sum determines their product.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: If the legs are $a,b$ and hypotenuse $c$, then $2c^2=12800$, so $c=80$ and $a+b=100$. Hence $2ab=(a+b)^2-(a^2+b^2)=10000-6400=3600$. The area is $ab/2=900$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: Real numbers $x,y$ satisfy $|x|+x+y=5$ and $x+|y|-y=10$. Find $x+y$.
ratingReason: The absolute values require a small sign split; the viable branch reduces to two linear equations.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: If $x<0$, the first equation gives $y=5$, contradicting the second. Thus $x\ge0$. If $y\ge0$, the second gives $x=10$, contradicting $2x+y=5$. Hence $y<0$ and $2x+y=5$, $x-2y=10$. These give $x=4,y=-3$, so $x+y=1$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: After Thomas tells his first lie, he repeats the pattern: two true statements, then one lie. Before that first lie he may tell zero, one or two truths. About a two-digit number he says, in order: “One digit is 2”; “It is greater than 50”; “It is even”; “It is less than 30”; “It is divisible by 3”; “One digit is 7”. Find the sum of its digits.
ratingReason: There are only three phases for the truth pattern. Comparing paired size and digit statements quickly eliminates two phases.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: The three patterns are FTTFTT, TFTTFT and TTFTTF. The second requires a number below 30 that is even and has digits 2 and 7, impossible. The third requires both greater than 50 and less than 30. In the first, the number is above 50, even, divisible by 3, has digit 7 and has no digit 2. It must be $78$, so the digit sum is $15$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: Three circles with centres $A,B,C$ and radii $30,20,10$ are externally tangent in pairs. Find the area of triangle $ABC$.
ratingReason: The sides are sums of radii, giving the familiar 30–40–50 right triangle.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: The side lengths are $50,40,30$. Since $30^2+40^2=50^2$, the area is $30\cdot40/2=600$.

competition: Colombian Mathematical Olympiad, Superior Selection Round
statement: Integers are written in the nine cells of a $3\times3$ grid. Entries in cells sharing a side differ by $1$, and the sum of all nine entries is $500$. Find the central entry.
ratingReason: Distance bounds from the centre restrict the possible values to a narrow interval, and the checkerboard parity pattern selects the unique even value.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: If the centre is $c$, the four side-neighbours differ from it by at most 1 and the four corners by at most 2. Thus $|500-9c|\le12$, giving $c\in\{55,56\}$. The five cells of the centre’s checkerboard colour have its parity and the other four the opposite parity, so the total has parity $c$. Since $500$ is even, $c=56$.

competition: Uruguayan National Mathematical Olympiad Final Level V
statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^{2017}\frac1{\log_k(2017!)}$.
ratingReason: Change of base turns the reciprocal logarithms into the logarithm of the factorial product.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Each summand equals $\log_{2017!}k$. Their sum is $\log_{2017!}(2\cdot3\cdots2017)=1$.

competition: Uruguayan National Mathematical Olympiad Final Level IV
statement: Points $A,B$ satisfy $AB=5$. Circles centred at $A,B$ with radii $3,4$ intersect at $O$. A circle centred at $O$ meets the first circle at $P_1,P_2$ and the second at $Q_1,Q_2$. Prove that $P_1P_2\perp Q_1Q_2$.
ratingReason: Pythagoras makes the two lines of centres perpendicular, while each common chord is perpendicular to its own line of centres.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: We have $AO=3,BO=4,AB=5$, so $AO\perp BO$. The common chord $P_1P_2$ is perpendicular to $AO$, and $Q_1Q_2$ to $BO$. Therefore those chords are perpendicular to one another.

competition: Uruguayan National Mathematical Olympiad Final Level IV
statement: How many positive integers $n\le2017$ make the fraction $(2n+3)/(n+7)$ reducible?
ratingReason: Subtracting twice the denominator reduces the gcd to a fixed prime, leaving an arithmetic-progression count.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: $\gcd(2n+3,n+7)=\gcd(11,n+7)$, so reduction is possible exactly when $n\equiv4\pmod{11}$. The values $4,15,\ldots,2017$ number $(2017-4)/11+1=184$.

statement: Let $a_1=7$ and $a_n=7^{a_{n-1}}$ for $n\ge2$. Find the final decimal digit of $a_{2021}$.
ratingReason: The last digit of a power of seven has period four; only the preceding exponent modulo four is needed.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Every $a_n$ is odd and $a_n\equiv3\pmod4$, since an odd power of $7\equiv-1\pmod4$ is $-1$. Thus for $n\ge2$, $a_n\equiv7^3\equiv3\pmod{10}$. The requested last digit is $3$.

statement: Positive reals $x>y$ satisfy $x^2+y^2=axy$, where $a>2$ is real. Find all possible $a$ for which $(x+y)/(x-y)$ is an integer.
ratingReason: Squaring the ratio expresses it directly in terms of a; imposing an integer value parametrizes every admissible case.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Put $m=(x+y)/(x-y)>1$. Then $m^2=(a+2)/(a-2)$, so $a=2(m^2+1)/(m^2-1)$ for an integer $m\ge2$. Conversely, for any such $m$, take $x=m+1,y=m-1$; these positive numbers realize precisely that $a$ and ratio $m$.

statement: Let $x=1+\frac1{2^2}+\frac1{3^3}+\cdots+\frac1{2024^{2024}}$. Find the integer $n$ such that $n\le3x<n+1$.
ratingReason: A simple geometric comparison bounds the tail sharply enough to place the scaled sum between consecutive integers.
notes: Restored from the individual review after removing the publication difficulty cutoff. Rating unchanged; statement and subject metadata checked against the source.
solution: Clearly $x>1$. For $k\ge3$, $k^k\ge3^k$, with strict inequality for $k>3$, so $x<1+1/4+\sum_{k=3}^{\infty}3^{-k}=1+1/4+1/18=47/36<4/3$. Thus $3<3x<4$, giving $n=3$.
